nameStory: The maritime sac spider gets its name from its coastal tendencies - 'maritima' means 'of the sea' in Latin. Like many sac spiders, it builds silky retreat sacs rather than traditional webs, earning the family their common name. This spider seems to have a particular fondness for the salt-kissed environments near our New England shores.
description: The maritime sac spider is a small, pale member of the sac spider family that prefers coastal areas. These spiders typically have elongated bodies with relatively long legs, giving them a somewhat delicate appearance. They're part of a group known for building silk retreats or 'sacs' where they rest during the day, rather than spinning traditional webs to catch prey. Like other sac spiders, they're active nighttime hunters that roam in search of small insects.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened body with a smooth, almost glossy appearance and proportionally long, slender legs

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No catching web - instead look for small, white silk sacs or retreats tucked under rocks, in crevices, or among vegetation

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in coastal environments, often near the high tide line where salt spray reaches

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active at night, running quickly across surfaces when disturbed; retreats to silk sac during daylight hours

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically less than half an inch, feeling lightweight if accidentally handled

habitat: Maritime sac spiders live up to their name by favoring coastal habitats throughout New England. Look for them in rocky intertidal zones, salt marshes, and dune systems where they can tolerate the salt spray and shifting conditions. They often hide under rocks, driftwood, or among salt-tolerant plants like beach grass and seaside goldenrod.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter retreats to begin hunting and mating activities along the coast.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both adults and juveniles can be found. Look for their silk retreats tucked into coastal vegetation and rock crevices.
seasonality.fall: Mating season continues, with egg sacs often placed in protected coastal locations before adults prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, overwintering in protected silk retreats under rocks or debris above the high tide line.

funFact: Despite living in one of the harshest environments a spider can choose - where salt spray, crashing waves, and shifting sands are constant challenges - maritime sac spiders have specialized kidneys that can actually filter out excess salt from their bodies, much like seabirds do!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pale sac spiders in coastal areas, but the maritime sac spider's preference for staying very close to the ocean helps distinguish it. Remember: if you're finding sac spiders inland or in forests, they're likely different species - this one rarely strays far from the sound of waves.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, the maritime sac spider is either extremely rare in our region or easily overlooked due to its small size and coastal habitat. Many sac spiders look quite similar, so definitive identification often requires expert examination.
compareHints: Compared to its inland relatives like the Canada sac spider or riparian sac spider, the maritime sac spider is distinguished primarily by its coastal habitat preference. While other Clubiona species might venture near water, the maritime species specifically seeks out salt-influenced environments. Most other sac spiders in the genus prefer freshwater areas, forests, or grasslands well away from ocean influence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Clubiona spiralis is most similar to other Clubiona species like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider, sharing the same general pale coloration and body proportions.
Unlike the Canada Sac Spider which prefers drier woodland habitats, the riparian sac spider sticks close to water sources.

Clubiona obesa stands out from its relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider by its notably thick, swollen abdomen - while other Clubiona species have more typical slender abdomens.
Among its Clubiona relatives in New England, the Kaston Sac Spider is most similar to the Canada Sac Spider but tends to be slightly smaller and paler.
Bishop's Sac Spider differs from its more common relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider primarily in its rarity and subtle coloration differences.
Compared to other Clubiona species in New England, the Canada Sac Spider tends to favor slightly drier woodland habitats than the Riparian Sac Spider, which prefers areas near water sources.
